title: Exception hierarchy (choosing what to catch)
hook: Every failure type in .NET hangs off System.Exception. The interview skill is knowing which types a worker should retry, which should go to a dead-letter queue, and which should crash the process.

blocks.text: All exceptions inherit from **System.Exception**. Below it sit familiar branches: **ArgumentException** (and **ArgumentNullException**, **ArgumentOutOfRangeException**) for bad inputs, **InvalidOperationException** for wrong state, **IOException** for file and stream problems, **HttpRequestException** for HTTP failures, **JsonException** for bad JSON, **OperationCanceledException** for cancellation, and **TimeoutException** for timed-out work. Catch the most specific type you can handle; leave **Exception** for true boundaries only.

entries.plainDefinition: The root of every throwable type in .NET. Carries Message, StackTrace, InnerException, and HResult.
entries.example: catch (Exception ex) — catches everything derived, use sparingly.

entries.plainDefinition: Thrown when a method receives an invalid argument. ArgumentNullException and ArgumentOutOfRangeException are more specific children.
Wraps a failure in a static constructor (.cctor). The type is unusable for the rest of the process.
entries.example: Thrown when static readonly config fails to load.

entries.plainDefinition: A queue where poison or repeatedly failing messages land after retries are exhausted.
entries.example: After three TimeoutException retries, send the message to the DLQ.

blocks.text: A message consumer is a **boundary**. Catching **TimeoutException** to retry makes sense. Catching **Exception**, logging, and returning success is silent data loss — the message disappears as if it succeeded. Static constructor failures become **TypeInitializationException** — you cannot retry that in-process without unloading the type. Knowing the hierarchy tells you what is transient, what is a bug, and what kills the type forever.

blocks.title: ApplicationException is obsolete
blocks.body: Do not inherit from ApplicationException as a policy. Use domain-specific names (LeaseExpiredException) only when callers catch by name. Most custom exceptions add no value over InvalidOperationException with a clear message.

sections.heading: How to choose catch versus bubble

items.title: Identify transient faults
items.body: TimeoutException, throttling (HTTP 429), brief network blips — log, retry with backoff, then dead-letter if exhausted.

items.title: Let programming bugs bubble
items.body: ArgumentException, NullReferenceException, InvalidOperationException from bad state — these need a fix, not a retry loop.

items.title: Handle cancellation explicitly
items.body: catch OperationCanceledException when (ct.IsCancellationRequested) and rethrow — do not treat shutdown as a failure.

items.title: Avoid catch (Exception) { return; }
items.body: Succeeding the message after an unknown failure hides poison data. Bubble or dead-letter with visibility.

snippet.label: Message boundary: retry known, bubble unknown
snippet.explanation: Line 10: TimeoutException is a known transient fault — log and rethrow so queue infrastructure retries. There is no catch (Exception). Programming bugs reach the host unchanged.

snippet.label: Specific types for specific failures
snippet.explanation: Line 7: JsonException is the precise parse failure. Line 9: wrap once with InnerException so the worker sees InvalidOperationException but logs retain the JSON detail.

snippet.label: Static constructor failure
snippet.explanation: Line 3: if LoadKeyOrThrow fails, the type initializer throws. Line 11: callers see TypeInitializationException — the type is broken for this process; retrying the same code path will not help.

blocks.title: Exception hierarchies in C# vs JS/TS
rows: Real type tree under Exception — catch by type
Error subclasses exist but many libraries throw plain objects
Ordered catch clauses approximate exhaustive failure handling
TS cannot exhaustively type thrown errors
Rare, named for domain, caught by type
Common but inconsistent — often just message strings
Unhandled thread exception can kill the process
Uncaught errors log; Node policy varies

blocks.title: catch (Exception) { return; } in a queue handler
blocks.body: The message is marked processed while data was never handled. Metrics look green; customers lose data. Rethrow unknown failures or route to a dead-letter queue.

blocks.title: Custom exceptions nobody catches by name
blocks.body: LeaseExpiredException that adds no properties and is never caught specifically is noise. Use InvalidOperationException with a clear message unless a caller truly branches on the type.

interviewTakeaways: Catch specific types; Exception only at a true boundary.
Workers: retry/DLQ for transient faults; bubble programming bugs.
TypeInitializationException means the type is done for this process.
commonPitfalls: catch (Exception) { return; } in an SQS handler.
Custom exception types that add no extra data and are never caught by name.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript has Error, TypeError, and user subclasses, but many libraries throw plain objects. C# culture expects a real hierarchy under Exception.
TypeScript cannot exhaustively type thrown errors. C# catch lists are the closest thing to an exhaustive failure story at compile time.
